newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean leading lawmaker admits taking Hanbo money.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean leading lawmaker admits taking Hanbo money.

text.p: A senior South Korean lawmaker from the main opposition party said on Friday he received money from the striken Hanbo steel group, but said it was not a bribe.
Kim Sang-hyun of the National Congress for New Politics told reporters the money was received as a political fund and he had not given any favours to the group in return for the money.
"I have received no more than 50 million won ($55,930) from the Hanbo Group, not from the group's founder Chung Tae-soo," Kim said before being led to a prosecution office for questioning.
"I have not given any favors because of the money. If the amount exceeds 50 million won, I will retire as a politician."
State prosecutors have begun to summon for questioning prominent lawmakers named by the founder of the stricken Hanbo Group as taking his money.
A prosecution official said Kim Yong-hwan, secretary-general of the United Liberal Democrats (ULD), was being investigated to find out if he had accepted money illegally from Chung.
The ULD is one of the two main opposition parties.

Kim Deog-ryong, a leading lawmaker of the ruling New Korea Party and a member of President Kim Young-sam's inner circle, and three other lawmakers would also be summoned on Saturday, the official said.

Kim Sang-hyun and Kim Yong-hwan are among 33 politicians, including 20 members of parliament, the prosecutors said they would question in the next two weeks in connection with a loans scandal involving Hanbo.
Analysts said the probe could lead to a shift in the country's political alignment.
"They include major figures and I am afraid this might touch off a political big bang," said a member of the ruling New Korea Party who asked not to be identified.
"The biggest casualty will be political apathy. If lawmakers are probed one after another, the credibility of political establishments will be seriously damaged," he said.
Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo and his aides have told prosecutors that they gave money to the 33 as "political funds" but denied bribing them, senior prosecutor Shim Je-ryoon said.
The prosecutors charged that Chung had bribed politicians and bankers to keep loans rolling into Hanbo's steelmaking flagship, which collapsed in January.
They alleged that Chung diverted millions of dollars from the bank loans earmarked for investment and used it to buy influence.
Among the 20 lawmakers are 13 from the ruling party, including Kim Deog-ryong, a member of President Kim Young-sam's inner circle.
Both Kim Sang-hyun and Kim Deog-ryong have said they want to run in presidential elections in December.
"I suspect there might be a conspiracy against me," Kim Deog-ryong told reporters, denying he took money from Chung.
Shim said his investigation team wanted to question the three senior politicians first as Chung told a parliamentary hearing this week that his aides had delivered his money to them.
Chung is on trial on bribery and other charges along with nine others, including three close associates of President Kim, in connection with the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co.
The parliamentary hearing, being broadcast live from a jail where Chung and some others are being held, sparked public calls that corrupt links between businessmen and politicians must be revealed.
